facts.fact: Indian almond (catappa) leaves are the dried leaves of the tree Terminalia catappa, native to Asia and Oceania and now grown throughout the tropics and subtropics.
As the leaves break down they release tannins and other weakly acidic compounds that slowly lower pH and tint the water yellow-brown.
Keepers use the leaves for soft, acidic-water fish such as Apistogramma, Betta splendens, gouramis, tetras, discus and crystal shrimp (Caridina cantonensis).
The leaves are common in hobby fishkeeping but are not used in commercial aquaculture.
As the leaf breaks down it becomes food for shrimp.
Leaves sold for aquariums are large dried leaves, about 4-7 inches (10-18 cm) long.
On the tree, Terminalia catappa leaves are 15–25 cm long and 10–14 cm broad, ovoid, and glossy, leathery dark green. They turn pinkish-red or yellow-brown before they fall in the dry season.
Fallen leaves for tank use are dry and brown or reddish-brown. The tank water turns an amber or tea colour.
Choose dry leaves that have yellowed or fallen and are reddish-brown.
The leaf is thick with hard veins, so it breaks down slowly.
Leaves float for the first 3-7 days. You can weigh them down with a rock or decoration.
Leaves float at first and then sink as they become waterlogged, usually within 24-48 hours.
A dried leaf floats at first and sinks after soaking.
Too many leaves turn the water dark, making the fish hard to see.
In soft water, tannins lower pH by about 0.2-0.5 units. In well-buffered water the effect is negligible, especially above KH 4-5.
Leaves lower pH more slowly than pH-buffer chemicals, which is considered gentler.
Tannins lower pH and may also soften the water.
Start with 1 leaf per 5-20 gallons. For blackwater, add more leaves plus softwoods such as Malaysian driftwood or cholla wood until you reach the colour you want.
Dose table for medium leaves (~15 cm): 1 leaf for 20-30 L, 1-2 for 40-60 L, 2-3 for 80-120 L, 3-5 for 150-200 L. Start conservatively.
Lá bàng: one dried leaf per about 30 liters of water.
Lá bàng khô: in large tanks, one leaf per 25–30 liters. Cut out the central vein first.
Lá bàng: about 10 cm of leaf per 4–8 liters of water.
Lá bàng: cut the leaf into small pieces, put them in a cloth bag in the filter, and replace the bag every 2–3 weeks.
Rinse leaves only if they are dusty or dirty. Do not boil them before adding them, because boiling releases all the tannins.
Rinse dirty leaves several times in clean water. For small tanks, cut the leaf in half or soak it in a bucket for a few days first.
Pre-soaking the leaves for 24-48 hours in dechlorinated water reduces the first burst of tint. Dry damp leaves in the sun for a day.
The leaves can be crumbled or cut small, rinsed and added directly. Blanching them first reduces how yellow the water turns.
A leaf usually lasts one to two months before it fully breaks down. Add a second leaf when holes appear in the first.
Replace leaves every 2-3 weeks. In shrimp tanks they can stay until only the leaf skeleton is left.
Lá bàng khô: replace leaves after about 5–7 days, because they decompose and can foul the water. For bettas, soak one leaf in about 5 liters for 7–8 days, then replace it.
To make an extract, boil one leaf per 0.5 gallon (2 L) of water in a pot you don't mind staining, then cool it before adding it.
Nước lá bàng: simmer 2–3 dried leaves in 1 liter of water on low heat for about 5 minutes, soak overnight, strain, then bottle and refrigerate for up to about 6 months.
Nước lá bàng: use about 10 ml per 4–5 liters of tank water after each water change.
Indian almond leaves are generally not used for high-pH fish such as African cichlids and many livebearers.
Too much extract can drop pH suddenly and shock fish. Fix it with a 25% water change or carbon.
Carbon in the filter removes the tannin colour, so leaving it in works against the leaves.
Fresh green leaves leave a film and sap. Leaves from young trees have more sap, so mature trees are better.
Green leaves picked from the tree have less tannin. Leaves from busy roadsides may carry exhaust pollutants.
Avoid leaves from pesticide-sprayed trees, and don't combine lá bàng with salt.
In lá bàng water, a large water change can raise pH suddenly, shocking fish and stopping them from feeding.
Leaving leaves in the tank too long can make the water rot.

The leaves have only very slight antibacterial and antifungal properties. Keepers use them for mild ailments, such as a betta that bites its own fins, and scientists are still researching these effects.
Research on extracts against Aeromonas hydrophila and Saprolegnia is mentioned without sources. Lower infection is only 'believed', and the leaves are 'not a replacement for proper medication'.
sera Phyto med Catappa is a Terminalia catappa leaf extract sold against external fungal, bacterial (including fin rot) and parasitic infections. Per the maker, 50 ml treats 400 liters (106 US gal).
sera says Phyto med Catappa is up to 10 times more effective than plain catappa leaves. This is the maker's own claim.
In a Can Tho University study, 70% ethanol Terminalia catappa leaf extract was safe for ornamental fish (Danio rerio, Melanotaeniidae, Gymnocorymbus ternetzi) at 100 µg/mL.
In the same study, a 75:25 blend of Terminalia catappa and Nelumbo nucifera extracts kept survival above 80% under oxidative stress and above 40% after infection with Edwardsiella ictaluri.
No study yet shows that lá bàng makes fish scales or skin harder (AquaSetup).
Sellers' claims that leaves kill parasites and bacteria and make arowana fins thicker are anecdotes, not tested results.
Leaves may lower pH and heavy metals and act against parasites, bacteria and egg fungus, but the article cites no sources for these claims.
In Vietnam, dried lá bàng sells for about 1,000 đồng per leaf, or 100,000 đồng/kg by weight. One Hanoi shop on Hoàng Hoa Thám sells 5–10 kg a day.
Vietnamese keepers buy the leaves for arowana (cá rồng), discus (cá dĩa) and cá thìa lìa.
Nước cốt lá bàng (Betta's House) is a bottled 330ml extract of 60% water and 40% fallen dried leaves, dosed at 1–2 caps per 1 liter. It keeps 2 months.
Betta's House sells its nước cốt lá bàng for soft-water fish such as cá dĩa, cá lia thia and betta, and to reduce stress during transport.
Vietnamese shops sell imported SunGrow Catappa leaves alongside locally collected dried lá bàng.

Do not use leaves that have been exposed to pesticides, road runoff or unknown contamination.
Adding too many leaves can darken the water so much that you lose sight of your fish before it becomes too acidic for them.
A shop page says to start with about 5-10ml of almond-leaf concentrate (nước cốt) for 10 litres of tank water, adding it bit by bit while watching the fish and the water colour.
The same page makes the concentrate from about 3-5 dried leaves per litre of clean water, simmered gently for 10-15 minutes or soaked overnight in warm water, then strained.
Another page suggests starting with about 10-20ml of prepared almond-leaf water for each 10 litres of tank water.
That page says to cool the strained almond-leaf water to tank temperature before adding it, to avoid temperature shock.
